content: Uterine fibroids are benign tumors composed of smooth muscle cells that develop in the uterus. These tumors are often associated with symptoms such as abnormal uterine bleeding, pelvic pressure or bulk symptoms, and reproductive dysfunction. Progesterone plays a significant role in the development and progression of fibroids, which has led to the exploration of selective progesterone receptor modulators (SPRMs) as a potential treatment option. Both clinical and biochemical evidence suggests that SPRMs can reduce the size of fibroids and alleviate associated symptoms. Importantly, SPRMs induce specific histological changes in the endometrium, which are benign, reversible, and not associated with cancer or precancerous conditions. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of SPRMs in treating premenopausal women with uterine fibroids. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and CINAHL, up to May 2016. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving premenopausal women treated with SPRMs for at least three months were included. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were performed independently by two reviewers. Meta-analyses were conducted using a random-effects model, with the primary outcome being changes in fibroid-related symptoms. The review included 14 RCTs with a total of 1,215 participants. Data from 11 studies involving 1,021 participants were included in the meta-analysis. Of these, 685 women received SPRMs, while 336 were assigned to a control group (placebo or leuprolide acetate). The SPRMs evaluated included mifepristone (five studies), ulipristal acetate (four studies), and asoprisnil (two studies). The primary outcomes assessed were symptom severity, health-related quality of life, abnormal uterine bleeding, and pelvic pain. Adverse events were primarily limited to SPRM-associated endometrial changes. Eight of the 14 studies were deemed to have a low risk of bias, while the remaining studies had limitations related to poor reporting of methods. The overall quality of evidence was affected by potential publication bias. When compared to placebo, SPRMs significantly improved fibroid symptom severity (mean difference [MD] -20.04 points, 95% confidence interval [CI] -26.63 to -13.46; moderate-quality evidence) and health-related quality of life (MD 22.52 points, 95% CI 12.87 to 32.17; moderate-quality evidence) as measured by the Uterine Fibroid Symptom Quality of Life Scale (UFS-QoL). SPRMs also reduced menstrual blood loss, although the effect size was small (standardized mean difference [SMD] -1.11, 95% CI -1.38 to -0.83; moderate-quality evidence). Additionally, SPRM treatment resulted in higher rates of amenorrhea compared to placebo (29 per 1,000 in the placebo group versus 237 to 961 per 1,000 in the SPRM group; odds ratio [OR] 82.50, 95% CI 37.01 to 183.90; moderate-quality evidence). However, no definitive conclusions could be drawn regarding changes in pelvic pain due to variability in the data. SPRM-associated endometrial changes were more common in the SPRM group than in the placebo group (OR 15.12, 95% CI 6.45 to 35.47; low-quality evidence). In comparisons between SPRMs and leuprolide acetate, two RCTs were included. One RCT reported primary outcomes, showing no significant differences between SPRMs and leuprolide in terms of quality of life improvements (MD -3.70 points, 95% CI -9.85 to 2.45; moderate-quality evidence) or health-related quality of life scores (MD 1.06 points, 95% CI -5.73 to 7.85; moderate-quality evidence). The reduction in menstrual blood loss, as measured by the pictorial blood loss assessment chart (PBAC), was inconclusive due to wide confidence intervals (MD 6 points, 95% CI -40.95 to 50.95; low-quality evidence). Similarly, no significant differences were observed in rates of amenorrhea (804 per 1,000 in the leuprolide group versus 732 to 933 per 1,000 in the SPRM group; OR 1.14, 95% CI 0.60 to 2.16; moderate-quality evidence) or pelvic pain scores (MD -0.01 points, 95% CI -2.14 to 2.12; moderate-quality evidence). SPRM-associated endometrial changes were more frequently observed in the SPRM group compared to the leuprolide group (OR 10.45, 95% CI 5.38 to 20.33; moderate-quality evidence). In conclusion, short-term use of SPRMs improved quality of life, reduced menstrual bleeding, and increased rates of amenorrhea compared to placebo, suggesting that SPRMs may be an effective treatment option for women with symptomatic fibroids. However, evidence from one RCT indicated no significant differences between SPRMs and leuprolide acetate in terms of quality of life or bleeding symptoms. The effectiveness of SPRMs compared to leuprolide remains uncertain due to insufficient evidence. SPRM-associated endometrial changes were more common in women treated with SPRMs than in those treated with placebo or leuprolide, but these changes are benign, reversible, and not related to cancer. Reporting bias may have influenced the findings of this meta-analysis. Further well-designed RCTs comparing SPRMs with other treatments are needed to provide more robust evidence.
